# Two Programs, One CSV Contract

Two languages, two processes, **no interop layer**. No pybind11, no ctypes, no subprocess call, no
socket. They meet only at files on disk, and the file format is written down as a versioned contract
with a stated rule for changing it.

> "The system is **two programs that never call each other**. They meet only at CSV files on disk —
> the *frozen contract*."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/ARCHITECTURE.md, 2026-07-10

```
instance_generator (Python)  ──►  CSV files (the contract)  ──►  mdvrp (C++17)  ──►  solutions
```

## What makes it a contract rather than just "we use CSV"

Three things, and all three are needed:

**1. The columns are specified, in one place, as the authority.** `ARCHITECTURE.md` §2 tabulates every
file, who writes it, and its exact columns — `point_type,point_id,node_id,lat,lon,demand` with depots
first, 0-based ids and depot demand 0; `node_id,lat,lon` for graph nodes;
`from_node,to_node,length_m` for directed edges. The document declares itself the source of truth:
"If code and this file disagree, treat the disagreement as a bug and reconcile both sides together,
then bump the contract version."

**2. Ownership is one-directional and explicit.** Python owns all level rules (`config.py`); the C++
side reads level parameters from the `.meta.csv` and **never hardcodes them**. That is the rule that
actually prevents drift — without it, two programs "sharing" a CSV quietly grow two copies of the
same constants.

**3. Changing it has a procedure.**

> "Edit this file first, update **both** the Python writer and the C++ reader together, and bump the
> version (currently **v1**). Never change one side alone."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/ARCHITECTURE.md, 2026-07-10

## Why it is the right shape here

The split follows the strengths cleanly. Python does the things with good libraries and no
performance requirement — download the road network with [[osmnx]], sample instances, render figures
with [[matplotlib]], generate the [[leaflet]] maps. C++17 does the thing that runs millions of times
— the GA and [[lazy-dijkstra-distance-cache]]. Neither has to be bilingual.

The cost is real and accepted: every exchange is a serialise/parse round trip, and there is no type
checking across the boundary beyond what the readers assert. In exchange, either side can be run,
rewritten or debugged alone, and the intermediate state is inspectable in a text editor — which is
what makes [[generated-audit-artifact]] possible at all, since `verify_reports.py` re-parses the C++
side's output without needing to link against it.

The same shape appears one project earlier in miniature: `first_project`'s C++ solver writes
`summary.csv` and `history_*.csv`, and a 278-line `generate_plots.py` reads them. Same rule — the
plotting script never calls the solver, the solver never knows plots exist.

## Where it leaks

The contract is honoured; the *documentation around* it is not uniformly. `mdvrp/README.md` and
`docs/design-notes.md` still describe a flat `output/solutions/{csv,txt}` layout after
`ARCHITECTURE.md` moved to per-solver subfolders, and `HOW_TO_RUN.md` names two scripts that do not
exist. The contract document itself stayed correct because it is the one file the procedure requires
editing first — the others had no such rule. See [[documentation-drift]].

Also note that the contract CSVs are **gitignored** — instances and graphs are regenerated, not
committed. Since [[osmnx]] no longer returns the original geography, the contract is reproducible but
its *contents* are not. The committed reports on the C++ side are the frozen reference instead.
